area: Identity provenance: how the acting user's identity reaches the database (API routes, service RPC calls, DB function grants, direct browser access, realtime)
summary:
The coworker's assumption holds on every path a normal request can reach. Every API request checks the bearer token with Supabase Auth (auth.getUser) on the server. The server passes the user id it gets back as actor_user_id to *_service functions, and only the service role can execute those. I found 135 route call sites that pass context.userId, and no route that reads a user id from the body, params, query or ordinary headers. On the database side, 0 of the 295 functions that take an actor_user_id argument can be run by a signed-in or anonymous browser request through the API. All 28 tables the browser can reach directly get the user from auth.uid() in their RLS policies, and a rolled-back test with a forged actor on audit_events was rejected.

There are five exceptions. None of them breaks tenant isolation on today's configuration, but two are a step away from doing so:
(1) Three SECURITY DEFINER functions in the internal schema app_private trust a user id supplied by the caller and are executable by everyone (PUBLIC): apply_owner_onboarding_update, reset_employee_onboarding_for_rehire (no permission check at all) and accept_employee_invitation_for_user. Signed-in users (the authenticated role) also have access to that schema. Today the browser cannot call them only because the data API exposes just public and graphql_public (confirmed: the API rejected app_private with error PGRST106) and pg_graphql is not installed. The cause is that the rule stopping new functions from being executable by everyone exists only for the public schema. apply_owner_onboarding_update also lost its 2026-09-08 revoke when it was dropped and recreated. The privilege tests only scan the public schema.
(2) Leftover direct write grants let a workspace owner, from the browser, re-point another member's membership to any account and change roles without going through the API. Confirmed in a rolled-back experiment. The web app never writes that table.
(3) A development-identity bypass in the workspace account service is switched off only when NODE_ENV is "production". It ignores the allowDevelopmentIdentity:false setting in the production entry file.
(4) Live-update broadcast and presence channels are public, so their payloads and the user ids they carry are not authenticated.
(5) Kiosk identifies the person by device cookie plus PIN. This is by design.

The API's rule layer is duplicated. There are 7 separate places that turn a token into a user and 20 local authorization helpers. 7 of those helpers skip the shared document-restriction check.

Token-taking services each call getUser themselves: document-lifecycle-service.ts:175,261; invitation-service.ts:295; onboarding-service.ts:341; availability-service.ts:29; account-security-service.ts:135; workspace-account-service.ts:155. No route zod schema has a user/actor/requester field. The only non-auth headers read are idempotency-key, x-newfork-workspace-id (a target, checked by the resolver) and x-cron-secret. Exceptions: the dev-token bypass (workspace-account-service.ts:151-153, app.ts:1180-1196, app.ts:988-1014 x-user-id header); kiosk device+PIN identity (kiosk-routes.ts:380-411, by design); scheduled-export cron acts as schedule.created_by (schedule-export-cron.ts:63,79) but re-checks active membership and the schedule.export permission at run time (schedule-service.ts:1289-1305).

findings.title: Internal definer functions that trust a caller-supplied user id are executable by everyone
findings.detail: app_private.reset_employee_onboarding_for_rehire(target_workspace_id, target_employee_id, target_membership_id, actor_user_id) has no permission check. It retires a person's onboarding requirements and deletes their employee_sensitive_identifiers and employee_private_profiles, for any workspace. app_private.apply_owner_onboarding_update(actor_user_id, …) takes the actor from its argument, then renames the workspace and completes owner onboarding. app_private.accept_employee_invitation_for_user(target_user_id, …) binds an invitation to a user id supplied by the caller. All three have proacl NULL, so PUBLIC can execute them, and authenticated holds USAGE on app_private. A rolled-back call as authenticated reached the function body. They are not reachable over HTTP today, only because PostgREST exposes public and graphql_public (confirmed, PGRST106) and pg_graphql is absent. Root cause: 20260908132000 set `alter default privileges … revoke execute` only for schema public. apply_owner_onboarding_update was revoked on 2026-09-08 (20260908187000:472), then dropped and recreated three times (20260921200000, 20260922000000, 20260922010000) without re-revoking. The guard tests (supabase/tests/function_execute_privileges.test.sql, public_roles_reach_no_table_directly.test.sql #4) scan only nspname='public', so they cannot see this. Hosted schema exposure was not verified.
findings.fix_shape: One migration: `alter default privileges in schema app_private revoke execute on functions from public`, plus revoke execute from public/anon/authenticated on the 3 functions. Widen the two catalog tests to public+app_private (definer and proacl IS NULL → fail). Leave: high / do: safe.

findings.title: Browser can rewrite membership identities and roles directly, bypassing the API
findings.detail: authenticated holds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes, and INSERT/UPDATE on 11 more tables. The web app writes only user_profiles and user_preferences, so all other write grants are unused surface. In a rolled-back experiment as the Meyhouse owner, a plain UPDATE (what PostgREST PATCH /rest/v1/workspace_memberships would do) re-pointed an active employee's membership to an unrelated account (rows=1). That pulls someone into the workspace with no invitation and no email match, and writes no audit entry. The same experiment changed two members' roles (rows=2). enforce_membership_role_change never checks user_id, and it lets admins edit manager and employee rows, so any holder of workspace.manage can do this. The INSERT policy is broken (42P17 infinite recursion, a tautology `existing.workspace_id = existing.workspace_id`). The actor is still auth.uid(), but the identity of the target user comes from the caller and needs no consent.
findings.fix_shape: Revoke INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE from authenticated on every table the web does not write, keeping user_profiles and user_preferences. Drop the matching write policies. Add a catalog test that no table except that allowlist is writable by authenticated. Leave: high / do: moderate (check the org-settings screens that read these tables still load).

findings.title: Development identity bypass in account service ignores allowDevelopmentIdentity
findings.detail: workspace-account-service.ts:151-153 resolves the token `development-owner-token` (and the admin, manager and employee variants) to user d9f43e62-e099-48e1-bc6f-a5aabe8e87d5 whenever NODE_ENV!=='production'. workspace-account-routes.ts:653-659 then treats that token as recently re-authenticated, and workspace-account-service.ts:182-186 skips the account ban. api/index.js passes allowDevelopmentIdentity:false, but that setting only gates app.ts, so on any deployment where NODE_ENV is not exactly 'production' the /v1/account/* routes (workspace list/create, closure, ownership transfer, account deletion) accept a well-known string as that user. build:vercel does not pin NODE_ENV, and Vercel runtime behaviour was not verified. There are two dev-token regexes and three NODE_ENV gates in different files.
findings.fix_shape: Delete the dev branch from workspace-account-service and workspace-account-routes. Pass the resolver's (already gated) identity into the service, or gate on the same allowDevelopmentIdentity flag. Leave: medium / do: safe.

findings.title: Realtime channels are public; identity in broadcasts/presence is caller-supplied
findings.detail: 7 DB functions call realtime.send(…, private=false) on shift-exchanges:<workspace>, and the API broadcasts schedule:invalidation:<workspace> (schedule-service.ts:1390-1410) with actor_user_id, location_ids, draft_id and changed_shift_ids. realtime.messages has 0 policies, and no web channel sets private:true. Anyone holding the public anon key and a workspace UUID can read those payloads and inject forged events. Presence user_id is chosen by the client (useScheduleViewerPresence.ts:77-99). cascade_notice has no server sender at all (grep finds none), so only a forger can trigger the toast that names an 'actor'. Verified by code reading, not by a live Realtime experiment.
findings.fix_shape: Use private channels (config {private:true}, realtime.send(…, true)) with RLS on realtime.messages keyed on is_workspace_member(topic workspace). Delete the dead cascade_notice listener. Leave: medium / do: moderate.

findings.title: The same identity/authorization gate is re-implemented per route file and drifts
findings.detail: There are 7 independent token→user resolvers and 20 local authorize helpers. The shared helpers in auth/workspace-context.ts check workspace match, active membership, documentAccess.restricted, onboarding complete and permission. schedule-routes managerContext/activeManagerContext, schedule-lineup authorize/authorizeActive, schedule-requests authorizeAny/authorizeAnyActive and onboarding managerContext call contextResolver.resolve directly. They skip documentAccess.restricted, and authorizeAny/AnyActive also skip membership.status. At the API layer this is the reported 'document-blocked manager can still write a shift'. Identity itself is still JWT-derived everywhere. Also: bearer parsing is case-sensitive in 4 copies and case-insensitive in schedule-lineup, and the cron-secret helper is copy-pasted 4 times with a non-constant-time compare.
findings.fix_shape: One exported authorize(request, {workspaceFrom, permission|anyOf, allowIncompleteOnboarding}) in auth/workspace-context.ts. Delete the 20 local helpers and the duplicate bearerToken copies. Add a route-matrix test that iterates app routes with a restricted, suspended and employee context. Leave: medium / do: moderate.

findings.title: Browser may write arbitrary audit_events rows as itself
findings.detail: The audit_insert_member policy pins actor_user_id to auth.uid() (a forged actor was rejected, E1), but any active member can insert audit rows with any action and target text in their workspace (E2 succeeded). This weakens trust in the audit log rather than identity.
findings.fix_shape: Revoke INSERT on audit_events from authenticated (covered by the write-grant cleanup above).

findings.title: Dead or fallback identity paths
findings.detail: The resolver's no-service-key fallback (workspace-context.ts:203, requestClient.rpc('resolve_active_workspace')) cannot work: authenticated no longer has execute on it. /v1/development/context (app.ts:988-1014) builds a context from x-user-id/x-workspace-id/x-workspace-role headers, and the web never calls it. The dev resolver (app.ts:1180-1196) grants owner permissions for any workspace id, so locally only the DB _service checks stop cross-workspace use. save_employee_hub_availability_service is a tombstone that only raises an error.
findings.fix_shape: Delete the fallback branch, the /v1/development/context route and the tombstone function (no live data, so no compatibility is needed).

findings.title: Some idempotency keys are not scoped to the actor
findings.detail: Unique keys on employee_acknowledgement_envelopes, lineup_operation_events and lineup_proposals are (workspace_id, idempotency_key), and on schedule_edit_session_shifts (session_id, idempotency_key). The 11 other command tables include the actor. Whether a replay returns another actor's result was not verified.
findings.fix_shape: Add actor_user_id to those unique keys, or assert the actor matches on replay. Verify with one pgTAP case.

implications_for_decision: Identity provenance is not a reason to rebuild. The core pattern is sound and is what a rebuild would produce again: the server verifies the JWT with Supabase Auth, runs as service_role, and calls *_service(actor) functions that nobody else can execute, with the database checking permission. It is applied consistently: 135 call sites, 0 browser-callable actor-trusting functions, and auth.uid() in every RLS policy. What is wrong is hygiene around that core. Rules (grants, revokes, gate checks) are declared again for each function and each route, and drop-and-recreate or copy-paste silently loses them: the app_private default-ACL gap, a revoke lost on a signature change, leftover direct-write grants, dev bypasses gated in two different ways, and 20 authorize helpers of which 7 skip the document-restriction check. That argues for 'consolidate in place + rebuild the authorization core': one API authorize(), default-deny grants enforced by catalog-wide tests (every schema, every table, every definer function), private realtime channels, and deleting dead dev and fallback paths. Every fix is a small migration or a deletion. None needs a data model change.

findings.title: Document block enforced only on some paths: a doc-suspended manager can still edit and publish schedules
findings.detail: document_actor_blocked is called only by service_actor_has_permission, can_access_location, is_workspace_member, workspace_role_for and 4 document functions. The explicit-actor families skip it: schedule_actor_*, communication_actor_*, service_actor_can_time/kiosk_location, service_actor_can_access_employee, can_access_employee, can_manage_employee_record. In the API only the 4 shared gates check context.documentAccess.restricted; the route-local gates (schedule-routes 82 sites, lineup, requests, onboarding) do not. E1 (rolled back): a blocked manager acquired an edit session and wrote a shift while can_access_location returned false.
findings.fix_shape: One actor-resolution step (membership active, workspace lifecycle, document block, access_class, permissions, scope set) used by every DB decision and by one API gate. It needs an explicit list of actions still allowed while blocked (own documents, account, own notifications). Delete the route-local gates.

findings.title: NULL/omitted location means 'anywhere' in 4 helpers; correctness depends on 56 callers remembering a second step
findings.detail: `target_location_id is null or ...` in schedule_actor_has_capability_service, schedule_actor_can_manage_service, schedule_actor_can_publish_service and communication_actor_has_capability_service. Some callers re-check per row (get_schedule_requests_service). Others stop there: delete_schedule_draft_service and list_schedule_drafts_service (E2: a Main-Dining manager archived a Garden-Room-only draft), the export schedule list/update/delete functions (created_by-scoped only), template rename/delete, update_scheduling_settings_service (org-wide rule change by a manager; see A #36-41). The dead 4-arg overload of list_schedule_draft_document_conflicts_service returns employee names for all locations; the API uses the 7-arg overload. service_actor_can_time/kiosk_location treat NULL as deny, so the same argument means opposite things across families.
findings.fix_shape: authorize() never accepts NULL as 'anywhere'. A separate scope_set(actor, ws, permission) returns the allowed location ids for listings and menus, and callers filter by that set (this also removes the per-row helper calls). Delete the dead overload.

findings.title: Drafts and edit sessions are workspace+week containers, so location-scoped authorization cannot be expressed for them
findings.detail: schedule_drafts and schedule_edit_sessions have no location. Any manager with schedule.manage anywhere can list and archive every draft of the week (E2). G found the same root in the lock and save data loss (G S3 / HATA-2: one lock per workspace+week, save deletes the actor's locations and rewrites only the session's). No single location answers 'may this manager act on this draft'.
findings.fix_shape: Make drafts, locks and sessions per location+week, or store the draft's location set and require ALL-in-scope for container actions. No live data, so this is a contained schema change done before or alongside authorize().

findings.title: Two helper families disagree on workspace lifecycle: a suspended workspace still accepts direct writes to some tables
findings.detail: is_workspace_member and workspace_role_for go through workspace_open_to_actor. workspace_has_permission goes through service_actor_has_permission, which has no lifecycle check. Experiment (rolled back): Employee Demo set to 'suspended'. The owner got is_workspace_member=f but workspace_has_permission(settings.locations.manage)=t. A direct UPDATE on locations affected 1 row; a direct UPDATE on jobs affected 0 rows, because the jobs SELECT policy uses is_workspace_member while locations uses can_access_location OR workspace_has_permission. schedule_actor_can_manage_service=t as well; only the API resolver (0 rows) blocks it.
findings.fix_shape: Lifecycle belongs in the single actor-resolution step. RLS policies call authorize() rather than choosing between two helper families.

findings.title: Three identity channels: explicit actor, auth.uid() via RLS, and auth.uid() via set_config impersonation
findings.detail: 345 functions take actor_user_id. The auth.uid() family (workspace_has_permission, can_access_employee, can_manage_employee_record, can_assign_employee_locations, can_access_location, is_workspace_member, workspace_role_for, can_manage_workspace) serves the 65 RLS policies. 45 '_service' wrappers call set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub', actor) and then run auth.uid()-based inner functions (save_employee_service -> save_employee, terminate_employee_service, set_employee_archived_service, ...). 16 functions mix both channels. A's #35/#46 regression shows the side effect: the impersonated uid makes a trigger (enforce_membership_role_change) take part in the authorization decision.
findings.fix_shape: One explicit-actor authorize(actor, ...). Rewrite the 45 impersonating wrappers to pass the actor. Keep a thin auth.uid() adapter only for whatever RLS surface is deliberately kept.

findings.title: Open direct-write RLS surface on 28 tables that no client uses, and it bypasses invariants
findings.detail: authenticated has INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes (policies use can_manage_workspace). Neither the web nor the API writes them directly. There is no trigger on membership_location_scopes. E5 (rolled back): an admin inserted a scope row for a manager at a location where the manager has no work assignment, and schedule_actor_can_manage_service went f->t. This contradicts the migration rule 'Manager location scope is a projection of employee work locations'. TRUNCATE is granted on 16 tables; PostgREST cannot issue TRUNCATE, so this is low risk.
findings.fix_shape: Revoke the unused grants (memberships, scopes, TRUNCATE). Either move the settings-catalog writes behind the API or have their policies call authorize(). Add a test that only an allowlist of tables is granted.

findings.title: important_dates: reads ignore location, writes enforce the ALL rule
findings.detail: important_dates_select_member uses is_workspace_member only; insert/update use can_manage_important_date (ALL locations in scope, non-empty for managers). E3: a Main-Dining manager read a Garden-Room-only date directly. The web reads the table directly. The schedule read model reads it separately through a service function, so there are 2 authorization paths for one entity.
findings.fix_shape: Serve important dates only through the read model and API, filtered by scope_set, or add a location overlap check to the read policy.

findings.title: Role and permission semantics diverge between helpers
findings.detail: (1) The employee permission whitelist is hard-coded in service_actor_has_permission (9 keys, including schedule.read), while schedule_actor_has_capability_service requires access_class in owner/admin/manager. So 'employee has schedule.read' is true through one helper and false through another. (2) No role-class filter in communication_actor_has_capability_service, service_actor_can_time/kiosk_location or can_access_location. The last relies on all_locations, which is still true on 5 of 6 employee memberships (G S18, A). (3) Rank checks exist only in can_manage_employee_record and can_edit_role. availability_actor_scope read has none (a manager can read another manager's or the owner's availability), and approvals have none (G S17). (4) membership.role and access_class are both read (0 drift today).
findings.fix_shape: authorize() takes access_class from one source (drop membership.role or make it a generated column), keeps employee-role limits in the role permission data rather than hard-coded, and applies one rank rule to every action that targets a person.

findings.title: Authorization decisions buried in onion wrappers
findings.detail: There are 40 *_base/*_legacy* functions. Entry points reach their first check at depth 0 (154), 1 (58), 2-5 (9). For example mutate_schedule_edit_shift_service -> _document_conflict_base -> _soft_audit_base -> _label_base -> _base, where schedule_actor_can_manage_service finally runs. 116 actor-parameter functions contain no check themselves. get_schedule_read_model_service_label_base holds a pasted copy of schedule_actor_has_capability_service. A reviewer cannot see from an entry point which rule applies.
findings.fix_shape: Every API-callable entry point calls authorize() at depth 0. Collapse the wrapper chains while they are touched (no live data, no compatibility needed).

findings.title: Empty-set and NULL semantics are inconsistent
findings.detail: can_assign_employee_locations with an empty or NULL array returns true for a manager (vacuous ALL). can_manage_important_date with an empty array returns false for a manager. communication_actor_can_control_announcement_service with an empty location list returns false unless all_locations. The time and kiosk helpers deny on NULL, the schedule helpers allow on NULL.
findings.fix_shape: Define empty and NULL once in authorize(): empty target set = org-wide, which requires all_locations.

findings.title: RLS policy typos (tautologies)
findings.detail: employee_offboarding_followups_select and employee_offboarding_shift_actions_select compare termination.workspace_id = termination.workspace_id (both dead policies). memberships_insert_bootstrap_or_manager has NOT EXISTS(... existing.workspace_id = existing.workspace_id), so the bootstrap branch only works when the table is empty across all workspaces.
findings.fix_shape: Delete the dead policies. Delete or fix the bootstrap branch; owner creation already goes through create_owner_workspace_service.

findings.title: Development identity resolver is fail-open on NODE_ENV
findings.detail: When NODE_ENV!=='production', a static bearer token development-<role>-token resolves to a context for the fixed user d9f43e62 in any requested workspace id (app.ts 326-331, 1180-1197). With the manager token the API context says manager while the DB actor is the owner. Whether hosted environments set NODE_ENV was not verified.
findings.fix_shape: Opt-in flag (ALLOW_DEV_IDENTITY=1) that defaults to off, plus a startup assertion that refuses to start with it on and a non-local SUPABASE_URL.

implications_for_decision:
Recommendation: rebuild the authorization core, consolidating in place. No full rebuild.

**Why the foundation holds**
- The identity and data model the checks read is consistent: membership, role with access_class, role permissions, derived scope rows, employee assignments. Composite tenant keys are covered by A.
- The actor is verified server-side through Supabase Auth.
- No actor-parameter function is callable by clients.
- 124 of 152 tables are closed to direct access.
- Every defect found here is one of three kinds: (a) the same decision written 12+ times at helper level and 51 times inline, with diverging semantics (document block, lifecycle, NULL/empty, role class, rank); (b) three identity channels plus route-local API gates; (c) wrapper layering that hides where decisions happen.
- These are fixed by replacing code, not the schema.

**Two contained model changes should come first or alongside, because authorize() cannot express them today**
- Drafts, edit sessions and locks must become location-scoped, or carry their location set. This is the same root as G HATA-2.
- The time-off request's single location should go, per G M2 D4.

No live data, so both are cheap.

**Shape of authorize(), from what exists**
- Signature: `authorize(actor, workspace, action, target) returns boolean or raises 42501 with a reason code`.
- Plus `scope_set(actor, workspace, permission) returns uuid[]` for listings.

**Actor resolution, done once**
- Active membership, with pending_activation allowed only for self-onboarding actions.
- Workspace lifecycle (interactive, or draft for the owner).
- Document block, with an allowlist of actions still permitted.
- access_class from one source.
- Permissions from role data (no hard-coded employee whitelist).
- Scope = all_locations for owner/admin only, otherwise derived locations.

**Target kinds**
- workspace (settings, roles, billing)
- location
- location_set (announcements, important dates, exports, publication scope; ALL rule; empty = org-wide)
- employee/person (ANY rule for read and person-only edits; rank rule manager<-employee only, admin<-manager/employee, owner<-non-owner; ALL rule or per-affected-location vote for cross-location effects: terminate, archive, job removal, time-off approval)
- shift (its location)
- draft/session (its location or location set)
- request (time-off: affected locations; swap: both shift locations, self-approval ban, rank)
- self (own employee record or user; holder/created_by ownership)
- document (via employee, plus self)
- announcement
- notification (recipient is self)
- kiosk device and time entry (location, plus own)

**Verbs**
read, manage, publish, approve/decide, archive/terminate, assign_locations (subset rule), grant_role (cannot grant above self), export. These map onto the 75 permission keys in 16 categories.

**What gets replaced**
- 12 helper-level location implementations, 6 employee-target implementations, 51 inline functions, 45 impersonating wrappers.
- 4 shared API gates plus route-local gates (82+ sites in schedule-routes alone).
- 65 RLS policies: 8 are dead; the rest call authorize() or are revoked.

**The matrix test**
The coworker's proposed matrix test is the right guardrail: role × scope relation (in scope / out of scope / multi-location / none) × state (active, pending, suspended, doc-blocked, workspace suspended) × target kind × verb. It needs manager fixtures, which do not exist today (the only manager rows are suspended or in the leaked FX workspace). E1-E5 in this report are ready-made matrix rows.
summary:
**Verdict:** The coworker's diagnosis holds, with corrections. The foundation (tables, verified actor, closed client function surface) is sound. Authorization is duplicated and inconsistent across four layers: API gates, two DB helper families, and inline logic. Model changes are needed only for drafts/sessions and the time-off location. The fix is to consolidate in place into one authorize() plus scope_set(), backed by a matrix test. No full rebuild.

**Census of the 718 functions** (all numbers measured 2026-09-23 at session start)
- 33 named helpers.
- 12 distinct location-scope implementations and 6 employee-target scope implementations.
- 51 non-helper functions with inline role/scope/permission logic; 24 of them call no helper at all.
- 56 call sites that pass no location, so NULL means "anywhere".
- 345 explicit-actor functions, none callable by clients.
- 45 wrappers that impersonate via set_config; 16 functions mix both identity channels.
- 40 *_base/*_legacy wrapper layers.
- 65 RLS policies, 8 of them dead because their tables are not granted to clients.
- 28 tables still granted to clients, some with write access.

**Experiments** (each a single transaction ending in rollback; workspaces stayed 6 and auth.users 12 before and after)
- **E1** confirms the coworker's first example. A document-blocked manager can't see the location, but acquired an edit session and wrote a shift. The API route-local schedule gates don't check documentAccess.
- **E2** confirms the NULL-location risk in practice. An out-of-scope manager listed and archived another location's draft through a location-agnostic check.
- **E3** confirms that the important_dates read policy ignores location while its write rule enforces it.
- **E4** shows that a suspended workspace still allows direct UPDATEs on locations but not on jobs. The cause is two helper families with different workspace-status (lifecycle) rules.
- **E5** shows that an admin's direct INSERT into membership_location_scopes grants a manager scope at a location where they have no work assignment. That breaks the rule that scope is derived from work assignments.

**Actor from the JWT (the coworker's caveat):** confirmed by reading the code. Caveat: a development identity resolver accepts fixed bearer tokens whenever NODE_ENV is not 'production'. Whether hosted environments set NODE_ENV was not checked.

**Already covered elsewhere, not redone:** A (three live and one dead copy of the "can the manager access this person" rule; the manager terminate regression; org-wide settings permissions widening a manager's scope) and G (the ANY vs ALL location rules; no rank check on approvals; one plan-edit lock per workspace+week causing draft loss). This census extends A: the RLS policies that use can_access_employee never run, because those tables are not granted to clients.

It rewrote created_by. It set lifecycle_status='deleted', closed_at and closed_by, and the table's own triggers then queued 1 workspace_retention_purge_jobs row. findings.title: The same permission rule is written in several places that behave differently
findings.detail: The database policies use auth.uid() helpers: app_private.can_access_location checks document_actor_blocked and workspace_open_to_actor. The service functions take actor_user_id and use other helpers: schedule_actor_can_manage_service checks neither and returns true when target_location_id is NULL. 29 functions read membership_location_scopes directly, and only 1 checks the document block. There are three can_access_employee variants: app_private.can_access_employee has no role check and 0 callers; public.can_access_employee is used by 8 dead policies and 7 service functions; service_actor_can_access_employee has 23 callers and differs on archived profiles and own drafts. 45 functions bridge the two worlds by setting request.jwt.claim.sub to the actor. findings.title: The same settings are written through two paths, and several tables are open to writes nobody uses
findings.detail: On Settings > Organization, locations, departments, jobs, important dates, shift types and shift labels are created, updated and archived directly from the browser, checked by the database policy with workspace_has_permission. Reorder, delete and scheduling settings go through the API and are checked with service_actor_has_permission. The API also has its own POST/PATCH for jobs and departments (apps/api/src/settings/jobs-management-routes.ts:57,137,201,298). Grants with no caller in apps/web/src: workspace_scheduling_settings INSERT/UPDATE (availability_enforcement, conflict_rules; the web uses /scheduling-settings), workspace_onboarding UPDATE (an owner could set status directly), membership_location_scopes I/U/D, workspace_memberships I/U/D, workspaces INSERT, audit_events INSERT. Experiments (rolled back): an owner inserted a scope row directly, and the employee then reached Garden Room (can_access_location=true). This breaks the rule that a manager's scope comes only from their own location assignments. An admin hard-deleted a membership, skipping the termination flow.
findings.fix_shape: Pick one path per entity: the API. Revoke the unused grants now. Then move the 6 Settings > Organization entities to API routes, or keep them direct but checked by the same authorize() helper.

findings.title: Scheduled schedule exports always fail: the server reads tables its role cannot read
findings.detail: revalidateScheduledExportCandidate (apps/api/src/schedule/schedule-service.ts:1263-1295) uses the service_role client and reads workspaces, workspace_onboarding and workspace_memberships. service_role has no SELECT on any of them. Experiment (rolled back, SET ROLE service_role) returned 'permission denied for table workspaces', and the same error for the other two. The call sits inside the cron's try block (apps/api/src/schedule/schedule-export-cron.ts:57), so every due scheduled export errors. This is the reverse of SEC-002: the code expects access the grants do not give. service_role holds column grants on locations (id, short_name, timezone, workspace_id), so the other direct reads work. Not observed in a running app.
findings.fix_shape: Replace those direct reads with one *_service RPC, or grant the needed columns. Add a check that every .from() table in apps/api is readable by service_role.

findings.title: Dead or broken policies left behind
findings.detail: 8 SELECT policies on employee_* tables (employee_profiles, employee_invitations, employee_events, employee_job_assignments, employee_location_assignments, employee_terminations, employee_offboarding_followups, employee_offboarding_shift_actions) have no matching grant, so they never run. Two contain an unqualified-column tautology: 'termination.workspace_id = termination.workspace_id' (migration 20260908106000:96). memberships_insert_bootstrap_or_manager compiles to 'existing.workspace_id = existing.workspace_id' (migration 20260817093000:227) and references its own table, so every direct INSERT raises infinite recursion. Also: app_private.can_access_employee has 0 callers; list_employees and get_employee_detail cannot be executed by any API role; and the AppShell realtime subscription to notification_inbox_items (apps/web/src/shell/AppShell.tsx:271-280) can never fire, because the table is neither in supabase_realtime nor granted.
findings.fix_shape: Delete them (no live data, no compatibility needed). Extend public_roles_reach_no_table_directly.test.sql to fail when a policy has no grant, a grant's policy errors, or a policy subquery references its own table.

findings.title: Some grants and channels sit outside what the guard test checks
findings.detail: (a) 16 tables grant TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER to authenticated, and the postgres default privileges in public still hand Dxtm to anon and authenticated for new tables. TRUNCATE ignores RLS. The Data API cannot issue TRUNCATE today. (b) Broadcast channels are public: realtime.send(..., false) in migrations such as 20260909020000, and the web uses channel names without a private flag. realtime.messages has RLS on and 0 policies. Anyone with the anon key and a workspace UUID can listen to or forge shift-exchanges:/schedule:invalidation: events and schedule presence (IDs and user_id only). (c) app_private definer functions that take a caller-supplied user id (accept_employee_invitation_for_user, apply_owner_onboarding_update, reset_employee_onboarding_for_rehire) are executable by authenticated. HTTP cannot reach them because config.toml exposes only public and graphql_public. The hosted project's exposed schemas were not checked.
findings.fix_shape: Revoke TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER, and fix the default privileges. Add TRUNCATE to the guard test. Move the broadcasts to private channels with realtime.messages policies. Revoke EXECUTE on the app_private user-id functions from authenticated and anon.

findings.title: Managers get an empty role list with no error when adding an employee
findings.detail: loadEmployeeReferenceData (apps/web/src/employees/employee-data.ts:215-240) reads workspace_roles directly. That policy requires roles.read, which the Manager role lacks (checked in workspace_role_permissions for Meyhouse). roles.error is never checked, and RLS returns 0 rows, not an error; an employee got 0 rows in the experiment. A manager would see no roles to choose from. The manager case was not run as an experiment.
findings.fix_shape: Serve the list of assignable roles from the API with the authorize() check, or add a policy for the roles a manager may assign.

implications_for_decision: This area supports rebuilding the authorization core. It does not support a full rebuild. The data model is fine: RLS is on for all 152 tables, anon reaches nothing, 124 tables are closed to the browser, and 191 of 202 tenant links carry workspace_id. The problems are in two places. First, a thin leftover RLS surface: 28 tables, 15 writable, and many grants nobody uses, including admin-level lifecycle writes and a cross-tenant link path. Second, the permission rule is written 3 or more times and the copies differ: RLS helpers on auth.uid(), service helpers on actor_user_id, TypeScript filters, and 45 claim-spoofing bridges. Most RLS findings are cheap in-place fixes: revoke grants, delete dead policies and functions, add 9 composite FKs, add a grant/policy matrix test. The recurring cost comes from having no single authorize() that RLS, the service functions and the API all call. Building that core, then deleting the variants, fixes the cause. A schema or database rebuild would redo the parts that are sound.
summary:
I made no changes: no repo edits, no git writes, and every experiment ran in one begin/rollback psql session. Counts were 6 workspaces (FX included) and 12 users before and after; the brief expected 7 workspaces, but 6 was already true when I started.

The coworker's structural claims mostly hold. RLS is on for all 152 tables, anon can read nothing, and 124 tables are closed to the browser; the 202/191/11 FK figures are exact for tenant-to-tenant links, of which 9 are single-column and 2 are two-column. The claim that access goes only through functions holds for the browser, not the server: the API holds BYPASSRLS and reads 93 tables directly from TypeScript. The important_dates read ignoring location is confirmed by experiment.

Of the 28 tables the browser can reach: 10 are gated by membership only, 11 by permission or role, 1 by location scope (locations), and 6 are self-owned rows or a global catalog.

Concrete risks found by rolled-back experiments:
- An admin can set the organization to deleted (a retention purge job gets queued), turn on Shift Hub, and rewrite created_by with one direct update to workspaces.
- An admin can link their own organization's membership to another organization's employee record (single-column FK, no trigger).
- Any employee can insert fake, backdated audit log rows.
- An employee sees important dates for locations they are not scoped to.
- An owner can widen someone's location scope directly, outside the assignment-derived rule.
- An admin can hard-delete a membership, skipping the termination flow.
- Any signed-in user can create an active workspace directly.
- A direct membership INSERT always fails with 'infinite recursion' (a grant that can never work).
- The scheduled-export check reads three tables the server role cannot read ('permission denied'), so scheduled exports always error.

SEC-002 itself is closed, but its 8 dead employee_* policies remain, two with a tautology bug. The permission and location rules exist in several differing versions: 29 functions read location scopes, only 1 applies the document block, and there are three can_access_employee variants. The recommendation is to consolidate in place plus build one authorization core; nothing here calls for a full rebuild.

area: ROLE SOURCE OF TRUTH: workspace_memberships.role compared with workspace_roles.access_class and workspace_role_permissions, the sync trigger, drift paths, API/web reads, and manager data and fixtures
summary:
The coworker is right that there is no drift today, but only half right that "a trigger keeps them in sync". The role class is stored twice: workspace_memberships.role and workspace_roles.access_class, reached through membership.role_id. The only guard is a_sync_membership_role_reference_trigger (BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF workspace_id, role, role_id ON workspace_memberships). It rewrites membership.role from the role's access_class, so the membership side cannot drift. Nothing guards the workspace_roles side: there is no UPDATE trigger, no constraint and no FK. A rolled-back experiment showed that one UPDATE of access_class produces a mismatch. After that UPDATE the three layers disagree with each other: the API context says "manager + schedule.manage", public.service_actor_has_permission says false (it reads membership.role), and public.schedule_actor_can_manage_service says true (it reads access_class). The app cannot trigger this today, because save_workspace_role_service refuses a class change ("Existing role experience cannot change"), so the risk is latent: it would come from a future migration or from the dead legacy function public.save_workspace_role.

Reads are split. About 39 DB functions and 5 RLS policies read membership.role. 37 functions read access_class. 11 functions read both in the same body; cancel_workspace_closure_service even does `coalesce(role.access_class, membership.role)`. The permission root service_actor_has_permission reads membership.role for its employee cap, so all 106 permission-helper functions and 39 permission-helper policies depend on it indirectly. API and web never read membership.role: context.membership.role is filled from role.access_class by resolve_workspace_context_service / resolve_active_workspace (packages/shared/src/index.ts:764).

Two bigger problems than the column pair showed up:
- **Direct writes bypass the role-change service.** workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes are directly writable by owner/admin through the authenticated grant plus can_manage_workspace policies. The experiment showed an admin can change someone's role with a plain table UPDATE, with no audit event and no employee event. Writing `role` alone is silently discarded. Moving someone manager→employee leaves all_locations=false and stale location-scope rows, so the employee ends up confined to the old manager locations.
- **The rules around a role are copied.** The employee permission allowlist exists in 3 SQL functions plus 1 TS constant. Role default permissions exist in SQL app_private.role_default_permissions, in the TS rolePermissions map and in the fixture list.

On manager data: outside the leaked FX workspace there are 0 active managers, 0 custom roles and 0 invitations. There is 1 suspended manager row, created on purpose by supabase/seed.sql:153 in "Suspended Demo". The Meyhouse fixture creates only an owner and employees. Tests do use managers, though: 59 of 131 pgTAP files build manager fixtures. No test asserts the role/access_class invariant.

Recommendation: no rebuild. Make role_id → access_class the single truth and make membership.role a projection the database enforces:
- add UNIQUE(id, workspace_id, access_class) on workspace_roles
- add FK (role_id, workspace_id, role) → workspace_roles(id, workspace_id, access_class)

Drift then becomes impossible by construction, and none of the ~76 reader functions has to change. Also revoke direct authenticated writes on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes, delete the dead legacy role functions, derive all_locations and scopes for every class, and move the permission allowlists and defaults to one SQL source.

Leak check: public.workspaces was 6 before and after my experiment, not 7 as the brief states; 5 without FX. auth.users was 12 before and after.

claims_checked.claim: Role is read from two places: some functions read membership.role, others role.access_class
claims_checked.evidence: By regex over pg_proc.prosrc in public/app_private/app (718 functions), with the name lists checked by hand. About 39 functions read workspace_memberships.role: 36 through `<alias>.role` or workspace_role_for(), plus 3 through a bare `role` (app_private.sync_manager_location_scope `role='manager'`, save_workspace_role_service `select role into actor_class`, prepare_employee_invitation_service). 5 of these are triggers on the membership table itself. 37 functions read access_class. 11 read both in one body, e.g. create_employee_command_service `actor.role = 'owner' or (actor.role = 'admin' and role.access_class <> 'admin')` and cancel_workspace_closure_service `coalesce(role.access_class, membership.role)`. Policies: 5 of 72 read membership.role directly (audit_select_admin, workspace_onboarding_update_owner, workspace_closure_requests_select_owner_admin and workspace_ownership_transfers_select_participant through workspace_role_for(), plus memberships_insert_bootstrap_or_manager `role = 'owner'`); 0 read access_class. The permission root public.service_actor_has_permission reads `m.role<>'employee'`, so the 106 permission-helper functions and 39 permission-helper policies also depend on membership.role indirectly. There is a third, partly overlapping axis: workspace_role_permissions is read directly by 22 functions and through helpers by 88.

claims_checked.claim: Today there is no mismatch between the two (0 rows)
claims_checked.evidence: `select count(*) from workspace_memberships m join workspace_roles r on r.id=m.role_id and r.workspace_id=m.workspace_id where m.role<>r.access_class` returned 0 across all 6 workspaces including FX (measured 2026-09-23, before my experiment).

claims_checked.claim: A trigger keeps them in sync
claims_checked.evidence: a_sync_membership_role_reference_trigger (migration 20260817213000_roles_permissions.sql:172) is `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF workspace_id, role, role_id ON workspace_memberships`. It sets `new.role_id := resolved_role.id; new.role := resolved_role.access_class`. It fires first alphabetically, before enforce_membership_role_change. It only covers the membership side: workspace_roles has no UPDATE trigger (only 2 AFTER INSERT grant triggers) and no FK ties the two columns. Rolled-back experiment E1: create a custom employee-class role, assign it, run `UPDATE workspace_roles SET access_class='manager'`, and the mismatch count becomes 1.

claims_checked.claim: Reading from two sources means a future drift risk
claims_checked.evidence: Experiment E1 (rolled back), after the drift: resolve_workspace_context_service returned workspace_role='manager' and permission_keys containing schedule.manage, so the API and web treat the user as a manager. service_actor_has_permission(...,'schedule.manage') returned false (membership.role is still employee). schedule_actor_can_manage_service returned true (it reads access_class). all_locations stayed true, so the manager would see all locations. No app path can cause this today: save_workspace_role_service raises 'Existing role experience cannot change', and the only function that changes access_class, legacy public.save_workspace_role, is EXECUTE-granted only to postgres and is referenced by no function, API or test.

claims_checked.evidence: Membership-side writers: accept_employee_invitation_for_user (sets role and role_id), respond_workspace_ownership_transfer_service (both), update_employee_membership_role_service (role_id only), set_employee_archived restore (role_id from snapshot), create_owner_workspace (insert), legacy save_workspace_role (role only), plus direct table writes. authenticated holds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on workspace_memberships, gated by memberships_update_manager = can_manage_workspace. Experiment E2 (rolled back, as Meyhouse's admin under `set local role authenticated`): (a) `set role='manager'` returned 1 row but the role stayed 'employee', so the write was silently discarded. (b) `set role_id=<Manager>` succeeded, with audit_events 1→1 and employee_events 0→0, bypassing update_employee_membership_role_service. (c) Setting it back to Employee left all_locations=false and 2 scope rows, so the employee is confined to the old manager locations.

Invitations and snapshots store role_id only. Owner transfer writes role_id and role together.

The API has 12 context.membership.role checks (communication-routes.ts, schedule-routes.ts, schedule-lineup-routes.ts, schedule-export-v2-routes.ts) and 1 access_class use (settings/roles-service.ts). findings.title: The role class is stored twice and only one side is guarded
findings.detail: workspace_memberships.role is a copy of workspace_roles.access_class, kept by a BEFORE trigger on memberships only. One UPDATE of access_class (migration or superuser) creates drift with no error. Experiment E1 then showed a three-way split: API context = manager with schedule.manage, service_actor_has_permission = false, schedule_actor_can_manage_service = true, and all_locations left true. The app cannot reach this today, because save_workspace_role_service refuses class changes.
findings.fix_shape: Two DDL lines and no function rewrites: `alter table workspace_roles add unique (id, workspace_id, access_class); alter table workspace_memberships add foreign key (role_id, workspace_id, role) references workspace_roles (id, workspace_id, access_class);` (default NO ACTION). A class change on a role that has members then fails, and a mismatched membership cannot exist. Keep the sync trigger to fill role on insert. Add one pgTAP assertion that the FK exists.

findings.title: Admins can change roles by writing the membership table directly, bypassing the service
findings.detail: authenticated holds INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes, gated only by can_manage_workspace. Experiment E2: an admin's direct `UPDATE ... set role_id=<Manager>` succeeded with no audit_events and no employee_events row. `set role='manager'` returned success but was silently discarded. So 'who may change a role' is written twice, in the enforce_membership_role_change trigger and in update_employee_membership_role_service, with different checks: the service requires employee_access.manage and a linked employee; the trigger does not. Admins can also insert membership_location_scopes rows directly and widen a manager's scope outside the 'derived from own assignments' rule (read from policies, not run). The insert policy has a tautology, `existing.workspace_id = existing.workspace_id`; it is harmless because the trigger re-checks.
findings.fix_shape: Revoke INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes from authenticated and drop the 3+3 write policies. All app writes already go through SECURITY DEFINER services; grep found no direct writes in apps/web or apps/api. Then the trigger's role-change branch can shrink to the flag-guarded paths.

findings.title: Location facts derived from role are not cleaned when the role changes
findings.detail: all_locations is normalized by b_enforce_role_location_scope for owner/admin (true) and manager (false) only. For employees it is free: seed.sql:443-456 gives an employee false plus a scope row, while the fixture and invitations use true. app_private.sync_manager_location_scope returns early for non-managers, so scope rows survive manager→employee (E2c: 2 stale rows, all_locations=false, employee confined). The service path sets all_locations=true, which hides the stale rows, but they remain.
findings.fix_shape: In sync_manager_location_scope, delete scopes when class <> 'manager'. In enforce_role_location_scope, derive all_locations for employee as well (or drop employee scopes entirely, per the model-G decision). Remove the employee scope row from seed.sql.

findings.title: The rules attached to a role are copied across SQL and TS
findings.detail: The employee permission cap exists in 3 SQL functions plus packages/shared role-permissions.ts:275, applied again in index.ts:773-777. Role defaults exist in app_private.role_default_permissions, TS rolePermissions (index.ts:181, used by the dev identity paths) and the 203-row list in the Meyhouse fixture. This is the concrete 'same rule written again and again' risk, more than the column pair.
findings.fix_shape: Keep the allowlist and defaults in one SQL place, e.g. columns on public.permissions (employee_eligible, default classes). Have service_actor_has_permission, save_workspace_role_service and role_default_permissions read from it. Make TS read it from the API or a generated file, and have the fixture call role_default_permissions instead of listing keys.

findings.title: Dead legacy role code that can reclassify roles
findings.detail: public.save_workspace_role changes access_class and writes membership.role; it is the only code that reclassifies a role. public.delete_workspace_role and the table app_private.bl051_role_grant_snapshot (0 rows, carries an access_class copy) are also dead. All are EXECUTE/USAGE for postgres only, and no function, API file or test references them.
findings.fix_shape: Delete them in one migration.

findings.title: The riskiest role scenarios never appear in local data, and the invariant has no test
findings.detail: Excluding FX there are 0 active managers, 0 custom roles and 0 invitations; the one manager row is a suspended fixture. The Meyhouse fixture has only an owner and employees. Tests cover managers (59 of 131 files) but no test asserts role = access_class, the sync trigger, or scope cleanup on a class change. About 97 of 111 test files that insert memberships pass only `role` and rely on the trigger to resolve role_id, so membership.role is the de facto fixture API. That makes dropping the column expensive and the FK route cheap.
findings.fix_shape: Add to the Meyhouse fixture one active manager (2 locations via employee assignments), one custom manager role and one custom employee role. Add one pgTAP file asserting the FK/invariant, scope cleanup on manager→employee, and that authenticated cannot write memberships directly.

implications_for_decision:
This area does not justify a full rebuild or a rebuild of the authorization core. The duplication is a denormalized cache: memberships.role has existed since the core migration of 2026-08-17, and role_id plus workspace_roles were added the same day. The database can make it provably consistent with a composite FK, 2 lines of DDL, without touching the ~76 functions that read one side or the other, the 44 policies, or the ~97 test fixtures. Dropping membership.role instead ('rebuild the core' in miniature) would cost ~39 functions, 5 policies, 5 triggers, seed.sql and ~97 test files, for no gain the FK does not already give.

The real, cheap-to-fix holes are two. First, direct table writes on workspace_memberships and membership_location_scopes, which bypass the role-change service and the derived-scope rule: revoke the grants. Second, role-derived facts (all_locations, scopes) that are not cleaned on a class change. The rule copies (employee allowlist ×4, role defaults ×3) support the coworker's 'same rule repeated' diagnosis and fit the consolidate-in-place path: one SQL source, read everywhere, plus an authorization-matrix pgTAP that includes an active manager and custom roles, which local data has never contained.

Verdict for this area: consolidate in place.

area: Test infrastructure (pgTAP suite, CI, vitest) and a concrete authorization-matrix test design

claims_checked.claim: Coworker: there is no authorization matrix test
claims_checked.evidence: None of the 131 files in supabase/tests generates cases from a role x scope x action table. The only table-shaped loop is roles_permissions_rls.test.sql:116, which unnests 4 settings permission keys.

Each probe ran in a subtransaction and a sentinel exception undid it, so the fixture stayed intact (3/3 target rows afterwards). The prototype found real divergences (see findings). I read four predicates; each has a different shape. service_actor_has_permission checks document_actor_blocked and membership.role and takes no location. schedule_actor_can_manage_service uses role.access_class, lets NULL pass, and has no document block. service_actor_can_access_employee uses the ANY-location rule plus a rank rule. service_actor_can_time_location has no NULL pass and no access_class check. implications_for_decision:
From the testing side, the pain comes from two things: the test harness and the same rule written in many places. It does not come from a broken database design. The red and brittle tests trace to hand-inserted fixtures, deferred triggers that never fire under rollback, no CI gate, and wording or signature pinning. A rebuild would carry all of these over unless the harness is fixed first. The prototype also shows much of the code already matching the target model (employee detail read is exactly M2). The divergences are specific: NULL location, D3 terminate, inconsistent deny signals, and predicates that disagree. That argues against a full rebuild and for consolidating, or rebuilding only, the authorization core.

Whichever option is chosen, build the authorization matrix first, because it is the acceptance test for all three:
- **Consolidate in place:** it is the safety net for folding 10+ predicates into one authorize().
- **Rebuild the authorization core:** the expectation function is the specification.
- **Full rebuild:** the actors, situations and expectation function carry over unchanged; only the call templates change.

**Concrete design** (one file, supabase/tests/authorization_matrix.test.sql, one transaction ending in rollback):

1. **World**, built through product entry points where they exist, then 'set constraints all immediate':
   - Workspace W with Kadikoy (K) and Besiktas (B), jobs Server and Cook, and a second tenant W2.
   - 14 actors, each with their own employee record where the model says so:
     - owner Olcay
     - admin Zeynep (record at K only, to prove org scope)
     - managers Ayse (K), Mehmet (B), Can (K+B), and Nur (no location, scenario S16)
     - custom manager-class role 'Shift lead' Nil (K) with employees.read and schedule.publish removed
     - employees Ali (K+B), Emre (K), Veli (B)
     - suspended manager Sami (K), pending_activation Pelin, removed Remzi
     - W2 owner Xavier
2. **Targets:** self, person at K, person at B, person at K+B, person with no location or excluded from schedule, a manager-rank person at K, an org-wide or NULL-location object, and a W2 object.
3. **authz_action rows** (about 45): action key, domain, surface (rpc or rls), the call template on the real entry point the API uses, the deny signal (42501 / null / empty / P0002), and which target kinds apply.
   - Schedule: read grid, write shift, publish, export, edit lock (per location and week).
   - Availability: read, manager note, the soft/hard setting.
   - Time off: read, decide with assignments at K and B, submit own.
   - Exchanges: read, approve each location's leg, request own.
   - Employees: list, detail, save, terminate, archive, change role, invite, approve preferred name, read private contact.
   - Documents: read, review.
   - Settings: general, locations, jobs, roles (including an attempt to grant more than one holds), scheduling rules including approved-time-off hardness, notification settings.
   - Owner-only: ownership transfer, close workspace, entitlements, assign admin.
   - Notifications: own inbox, act on another person's item, own preferences.
   - Direct reads, as 'set local role authenticated' plus JWT claims, on the 28 tables that role can read.
4. **pg_temp.expected(actor, action, target)** returns 'allow', 'deny' or 'decide:<question id>'. It is about 60 lines of CASE and is the ONLY place decisions live:
   - other tenant, or status other than active: deny
   - owner-only action: owner only
   - owner and admin: allow
   - employee: own self-service actions only
   - manager, settings write: deny (D1); settings read: allow
   - manager, person actions: any shared location and the target is employee rank (M2 rules 1, 4, 5)
   - manager, cross-location person actions such as terminate or archive: all of the target's locations must be in scope (D3)
   - manager, shift actions: the location must be in scope; NULL means deny
   - custom roles: deny wherever the role has the permission removed
5. **Probe** (plpgsql): run the call inside BEGIN/EXCEPTION.
   - A NULL or empty result on a read means 'hidden'.
   - On success, raise sentinel SQLSTATE 'TA001' so the cell is undone and every cell sees the same fixture. Never use a code ending in 000: it matches the whole class, and my first prototype reported allow for every cell because of that.
   - 42501 or the action's deny signal means 'deny'.
   - Any other SQLSTATE fails the cell as a broken probe. This catches payload rot and validation that runs before authorization.
6. **Emit the checks:** select is(probe, expected, label) over actors x actions x targets. 'decide' cells go through pgTAP todo, so the open product questions print as a live list without failing.
7. **Consistency layer:** all location predicates must agree for each (actor, location incl. NULL).
8. **Coverage sweep:** every public *_service function whose arguments include an actor must be in authz_action or in authz_exempt with a reason. A new endpoint then fails CI until someone records its rule.

**What it replaces:**
- Roughly 300-350 of the ~476 authorization assertions spread across 99 files.
- The 106 per-function grant checks, which collapse into 1 sweep.
- About 80-120 stay, because they test something else: lease theft, spoofing, idempotency, row-shape leaks.

**How it keeps tests in step with decisions:** a decision changes one line in expected(). The next run lists exactly which cells flip, which is the impact report. Code is changed until green, and there are no fixtures to re-edit.

**What it cannot catch:**
- web and API gating (the 64 and 31 TypeScript checks, e.g. the Employee Hub route)
- API wiring and where the actor id comes from (it trusts the API to pass the JWT user)
- fields leaking inside an allowed response (e.g. private_contact)
- eligibility rules (location + job + availability), which need a second matrix on the same engine
- notification recipients (BL-099)
- lock and concurrency data loss (BL-097)
- a wrong expectation: the matrix enforces whatever expected() says, but visibly in one place

It needs the CI database job to have any lasting effect.

I read the pgTAP suite, CI and vitest, queried the catalog, and ran four rolled-back experiments. Every experiment was in one transaction ending in rollback; workspaces stayed at 6 and auth.users at 12 before and after, not the 7 the brief expects, and FX was untouched.

The coworker is right on both counts: there is no authorization matrix, and there is no realistic manager data. The second is worse than stated:
- **Manager scope is never really tested.** The sync that gives a manager their locations only runs at commit, and every pgTAP file ends in rollback. So 57 of the 59 files that create a manager test either a hand-made scope that the product would erase (40 files, shown by experiment) or no scope at all (17).
- **Nothing database-related runs in CI.** The only CI tests that look at the database regex old migration files. One is green while the real pgTAP check of the same property fails (verified by running it).
- **Fixtures are hand-built rows.** There are 1,242 raw inserts; memberships are inserted by hand in 111 files and 48 files depend on seed.sql. Every rule change therefore breaks dozens of files at their first fixture line. This is the mechanism behind "tests don't stay in step with decisions".
- **Tests check wording and structure.** 34% of expected-error checks pin exact message text, 106 grant checks pin function signatures, and 12 files depend on today's date (8 of them red).
- **Coverage of the hard cases is thin.** Admin, suspended, pending, custom narrowed roles and the two-location employee barely appear.

A prototype of the matrix works and is fast: 117 cells in about 0.5 s, each cell undone by a sentinel exception. It already found real differences from the target model:
- A NULL location passes 3 of 4 location checks, and those checks disagree with each other.
- A Kadikoy manager can terminate a Kadikoy+Besiktas employee, where D3 says admin or owner.
- The database says "no" in four shapes (42501, NULL, not-found, and a validation error that hides the scope check).

The design above puts every decision in one expectation function and runs 14 actors x ~45 actions x 8 target kinds as a single generated file. Open decisions show up as todo cells. A coverage sweep stops new endpoints from going untested. It would replace roughly 300-350 of the ~476 scattered authorization checks, plus 106 grant checks. It cannot see what screens and the API gate, fields leaking inside allowed responses, eligibility, who gets notified, or lock bugs.

From the testing side, the evidence points to fixing the test harness and consolidating the authorization core, not a full rebuild. The matrix should come first under any option. area: REBUILD COST INVENTORY: full rebuild vs a targeted rebuild of authorization, parallel systems and legacy code (main cf7dff4, local DB with 319/319 migrations)
summary:
Verdict: do not rebuild the whole foundation. Rebuild the authorization core, delete the parallel systems, collapse the legacy layers, and squash the migrations into one fresh baseline. Keep the domain tables.

What was measured (catalog queries run in rolled-back sessions, plus code reading):
- **Database:** 152 public tables (plus 6 app_private tables and 1 view), 718 functions, 639 of them SECURITY DEFINER, 26.6k lines of function code, 139 triggers, 72 policies, 52 enums.
- **Migrations and tests:** 319 migrations with 66,827 lines. A schema-only dump of the live schema is 54,845 lines. There are 131 pgTAP files with 4,275 assertion calls.
- **API:** 288 routes, 22 service modules (6.8k lines), 193 distinct RPC names.
- **Web:** 20 `*-data.ts` modules and 85k lines. It is tightly coupled to database shapes: 439 shared zod schemas with 1,321 snake_case keys, and 3,495 snake_case field reads across 168 web files. API services parse the plpgsql JSON and pass it straight through.

Class 1, the domain model (about 110 tables), is sound:
- 191 of 202 tenant-to-tenant FKs are composite.
- RLS is on for all 152 tables.
- Agent G found that model M2 needs essentially one schema change (the `location_id` on time-off requests), plus the plan-edit lock index.

Class 2, authorization, is where the foundation is actually flawed:
- There are two authorization styles. 284 functions take an `actor_user_id` parameter; 39 read `auth.uid()`. 45 functions connect the two by overwriting the JWT user claim inside the transaction (`set_config('request.jwt.claim.sub', ...)`).
- Location scope is implemented separately in 16 boolean helpers, and 29 functions read the scope table directly. On top of that sit about 20 domain helpers and 15 separate `authorize()` functions in the API.
- The helpers disagree. Two schedule helpers let a NULL location pass and skip the document-block check. Role is read from `membership.role` in one place and `access_class` in another.
- 8 RLS policies are dead because the browser has no grant for them.

Class 3, parallel or half-finished systems, is 36 tables:
- old availability: 8
- the old Requests shift-change flow: 3
- kiosk: 6 and time tracking: 8, both outside the MVP
- Line Up: 11
No table has ever been dropped: 158 were created and 158 still exist.

Class 4, leftover legacy code:
- 36 `_base` wrapper layers (2,365 lines). `mutate_schedule_edit_shift_service` is 5 layers deep.
- 407 function rewrites across the migrations.
- 3 tombstone functions, about 20–30 functions with no caller, 11 `_v2`/`_v3` duplicates, and settings stored twice and kept in sync by a trigger.

The BL-070 bugs trace to classes 2, 3 and 4, to missing CI, or to product decisions. None needs a new domain model.
- pgTAP is not part of CI: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs lint, typecheck, unit tests and build, but not `test:db`. That is why 38 red files built up unseen.
- 13 of the 31 red files outside Line Up are simply out-of-date tests.

The strongest warning against a full rebuild: this repo already is one. The first commit, 90f0fad on 2026-08-18, is titled "Initial clean rebuild foundation". The generation before it (C:/Users/TheWe/newfork: 569 migrations, 3,094 commits, April 21 to August 16) came with a written brief:
- It forbade kiosk and time tracking. Both came back (14 tables).
- It required every permission check to include location scope, ruled out SECURITY DEFINER as a shortcut, and asked for owner/admin/manager/employee test users.
Within 5 weeks the same kinds of defects returned. A pace of 58% of all migration lines written in 3 days (Sep 7–9) shows that writing code with AI is cheap. Making and enforcing decisions is the real bottleneck.

Estimates, in person-weeks for a solo developer with AI help:
- **Targeted option:** 6–11.5 person-weeks for authorization plus parallel systems plus legacy code plus squash, and 1.5–3 more for the M2 domain changes that any option needs. Total about 8–14.
- **Full rebuild:** about 13–24 person-weeks, and it only comes out better if the same authorization core, matrix test and CI gate are built anyway.

The coworker's review is mostly confirmed. Two corrections:
- "No manager rows" is wrong: there is 1 manager and 1 admin membership outside FX, and 59 pgTAP files create manager fixtures.
- A single `authorize()` is more than a consolidation. It is a rebuild of the authorization core, because two authorization styles and 16 scope implementations are a foundation flaw.

The caveat is resolved (checked by reading code): `actor_user_id` is taken server-side from `auth.getUser(accessToken)` (`apps/api/src/auth/workspace-context.ts`), and 151 of 151 route-level uses pass `context.userId`. The browser can execute only 6 public functions, and none of them takes an actor parameter.

Baseline anomaly: at the start of this session `public.workspaces` held 6 rows including FX, not the 7 the task expected. auth.users held 12. Both were unchanged at the end, and this session wrote nothing.
